metadata.title: The impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on academic performance are still a debated topic in public and empirical educational research, as the pandemic-related school closures have impacted approximately 90% of students globally (UNESCO, 2020).

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 microdata merged into a combined dataset with an added “cycle” indicator. Participants are 15-year-old students selected via PISA’s stratified sampling design (schools first, then students within schools). For the meta-analytic country-level models, the authors state that sampling weights and plausible values were applied in line with OECD recommendations, and they implement this using the R package BIFIEsurvey. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty quantification is described through meta-analytic variance components rather than replicate-based standard errors.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports that PISA provides ten plausible values and that all ten plausible values were utilized, but it does not describe any additional missing-data handling strategy for the analytic variables (e.g., ESCS, country indices) beyond the standard PISA framework. This omission is a reporting gap because missingness can affect ESCS availability and the merged country-level moderation variables (HDI/DRI), and the authors do not specify whether cases with missing covariates were excluded or imputed.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 scientific literacy domain data for 15-year-old students across 69 participating countries; one country was excluded due to inconsistent data that did not meet criteria for reliable interpretation. The manuscript does not specify further student-level exclusions (e.g., missing ESCS) or additional task/module filters beyond the standard PISA scientific literacy assessment and the merging of the two cycles.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 & 2022 (Science) — scientific literacy (15-year-olds, pooled across 69 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Scientific literacy (Plausible Values) — main effect of SES
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis summary effect: β = 0.28, 95% CI [0.25, 0.31]; heterogeneity I2 = 68.72; between-study variance τ2 = 0.0093 (95% CI [0.006, 0.0158]); Q(68) = 219.19, p < .0001
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 & 2022 (Science) the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS) and PISA cycle to predict scientific literacy (Plausible Values), finding that ESCS had a significant positive association with scientific literacy (β = 0.28). This indicates that strengthening equity-oriented supports for students from lower-SES backgrounds may improve scientific literacy outcomes, though the design remains cross-sectional across independent samples and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 & 2022 (Science) — scientific literacy (15-year-olds, pooled across 69 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Scientific literacy (Plausible Values) — interaction of SES with PISA cycle
main_findings.performance_metrics: Interaction effect: β = 0.06, 95% CI [0.03, 0.09]; heterogeneity I2 = 64.99 (as reported); between-study variance τ2 = 0.0080 (95% CI [0.049, 0.0150] as reported); Q(68) = 194.11, p < .0001
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 & 2022 (Science) the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS) and PISA cycle to predict scientific literacy (Plausible Values), finding a significant SES×cycle interaction (β = 0.06) indicating a stronger SES gradient in 2022 than in 2018. This indicates that pandemic-era disruptions likely widened socioeconomic inequalities in science learning, supporting policy priorities for targeted recovery and sustained equity interventions in scientific literacy.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA scientific literacy for 15-year-olds using pooled data from the 2018 and 2022 cycles across 69 countries (N = 1,060,311), treating each country as an independent “study” in a random-effects meta-analytic framework. Scientific literacy is modeled using PISA’s ten plausible values, and sampling weights are incorporated via OECD-aligned procedures implemented in R (BIFIEsurvey and metafor). The main effect shows a positive SES–science association (β = 0.28, 95% CI [0.25, 0.31]) with substantial between-country heterogeneity (I2 = 68.72). The SES×cycle interaction is also significant (β = 0.06, 95% CI [0.03, 0.09]), suggesting the SES gradient was more pronounced in 2022 than in 2018. Country-level moderation by HDI and DRI is not significant, and the authors emphasize that PISA is cross-sectional, so changes cannot be interpreted as causal pandemic effects for individuals.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical machine-learning prediction paper: the analysis uses linear regression and meta-analytic techniques (random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression) rather than training ML algorithms. Consequently, ml_techniques is intentionally empty and main_findings capture the regression/meta-analytic effects on scientific literacy rather than ML model performance.
